lessons.name: Identify the narrative point of view

header.text: <instructions>Which narrative point of view is shown in the passage?</instructions>

contents.text: Of all the countless things my son and I learned from the Professor, the meaning of the square root was among the most important. No doubt he would have been bothered by my use of the word countless—too sloppy, for he believed that the very origins of the universe could be explained in the exact language of numbers—but I don't know how else to put it.
<citation>From Yōko Ogawa, The Housekeeper and the Professor. Copyright 2003 by Yōko Ogawa</citation>
Narrative point of view describes the perspective from which the story is told. There are three primary points of view:

header.text: In first-person, the narrator uses first-person pronouns, such as I, me, we, and us, to describe events from his or her own perspective.

contents.text: I pressed my ear to the door, hoping to make out what she was saying.

header.text: In second-person, the narrator uses second-person pronouns, such as you and your, to directly address the reader, casting the reader as a character in the story.

contents.text: You brush a handful of crumbs onto the floor and slide into the diner booth.

header.text: In third-person, the narrator uses third-person pronouns, such as he, she, him, and her, as well as characters' names to describe events from the perspective of an outside observer.
With a third-person-limited point of view, the observer's knowledge is limited to what a single character knows and feels.

contents.text: Looking at the excited expressions of the other performers, Andrea saw a reflection of her own happy, fluttery nerves.

header.text: With a third-person-omniscient point of view, the observer is all-knowing and often reveals multiple characters' thoughts and feelings.

contents.text: Robert felt his hands tremble as he placed his hands on the piano's keys, but Ms. Keening already knew he would play the piece flawlessly.

But you think perhaps you can smell caramel wafting through the evening breeze, beneath the crisp scent of the autumn leaves.…The people around you are growing restless from waiting, a sea of shuffling feet, murmuring about abandoning the endeavor in search of someplace warmer to pass the evening. You yourself are debating departing when it happens.
<citation>From Erin Morgenstern, The Night Circus. Copyright 2011 by Erin Morgenstern</citation>

Narrative point of view describes the perspective from which the story is told. There are three primary points of view:

header.text: In first-person, the narrator uses first-person pronouns, such as I, me, we, and us, to describe events from his or her own perspective.

contents.text: I pressed my ear to the door, hoping to make out what she was saying.

header.text: In second-person, the narrator uses second-person pronouns, such as you and your, to directly address the reader, casting the reader as a character in the story.

contents.text: You brush a handful of crumbs onto the floor and slide into the diner booth.

header.text: In third-person, the narrator uses third-person pronouns, such as he, she, him, and her, as well as characters' names to describe events from the perspective of an outside observer.
With a third-person-limited point of view, the observer's knowledge is limited to what a single character knows and feels.

contents.text: Looking at the excited expressions of the other performers, Andrea saw a reflection of her own happy, fluttery nerves.

header.text: With a third-person-omniscient point of view, the observer is all-knowing and often reveals multiple characters' thoughts and feelings.

header.text: A clause is a group of words that contains both a subject and predicate. A clause can function as a complete sentence or combine with other clauses to form compound or complex sentences.

sentences.text: Samantha grew up in a bilingual family, so she can speak two languages fluently.
The clause has a subject (she) and a predicate (can speak two languages fluently).
The Hall of Records, which is found behind Mount Rushmore, contains copies of historical United States documents.
The clause has a subject (which) and a predicate (is found behind Mount Rushmore).

header.text: A phrase is any group of words that function together in a sentence but lack a subject, a predicate, or both.

sentences.text: We washed the dishes in the sink after dinner.
The phrase does not contain a subject.
The new physician at the hospital has been working long hours.
The phrase does not contain a predicate.
Robert and Emily took detailed notes during the lecture on microbiology.
The phrase contains neither a subject nor a predicate.

header.text: A clause is a group of words that contains both a subject and predicate. A clause can function as a complete sentence or combine with other clauses to form compound or complex sentences.

sentences.text: Samantha grew up in a bilingual family, so she can speak two languages fluently.

The Hall of Records, which is found behind Mount Rushmore, contains copies of historical United States documents.
The clause has a subject (which) and a predicate (is found behind Mount Rushmore).

header.text: A phrase is any group of words that function together in a sentence but lack a subject, a predicate, or both.

sentences.text: We washed the dishes in the sink after dinner.
The phrase does not contain a subject.
The new physician at the hospital has been working long hours.
The phrase does not contain a predicate.
Robert and Emily took detailed notes during the lecture on microbiology.
The phrase contains neither a subject nor a predicate.

header.text: <instructions>Read the story.</instructions>

passage.text: Mercy stirred the cornmeal mush, standard breakfast fare at Seely's Tavern. Nearby, her mother plucked a chicken for the midday stew. Their silence was companionable; neither was inclined toward conversation for its own sake, particularly this early. Soon enough, the tavern would echo with scraping, chewing, clattering, and, most likely, arguing. For now, they both relished the quiet.
When the mush was butter-smooth, Mercy rose from the hearth and lifted the egg basket from its hook.
"Best wait," Mother said. With Mr. Seely not yet returned from trading, she was more vigilant than usual.
"It's full morning," Mercy responded. "The fog makes it look darker than it is."

Mrs. Seely pressed her lips together but nodded, and Mercy stepped into the gloomy morning. Once in the barn, she tossed grain to the chickens, then pulled her poem from her apron pocket for yet another read. Entitled "Appeal," it was a direct address to the odd weather of late:

lines.text: Mornings dark with heavy fog, skies so pale and sallow!
Why the strange and reddened sun, upon this land so fallow?
Shall you steal away our blue? Farewell, blue sky and bluebell?
Save it for the Patriots' coats? Must even you rebel?

passage.text: Mercy frowned; it was terrible. She should throw it to the chickens. Absolutely, she could never show this drivel to John. Not that John was such a graceful poet, but Mercy didn't want him to think she wasn't.

She had met him last week, when he passed through Dole with the rest of his company. They'd taken their midday meal at the tavern, all of them dressed in their tattered Continental Army uniforms. As usual, the conversation at the table was insufferable, with the men braying like donkeys about freedom and slaughter. When Mr. Seely ventured that perhaps even freedom wasn't worth such bloodshed, John puffed out his chest and proclaimed, "No redcoat could spill my blood!"
"How can one not comprehend one's own vulnerability?" Mercy muttered, gathering the wooden bowls. She was speaking to herself, but John had heard, and his eyes met hers. She took the bowls and fled.
He found her later, when she was banking up the hearth. "Begging your pardon, miss," he said. His face was shy, the bluster gone. He handed her a folded paper, touched his hat, and left.
The note contained three scribbled lines.

lines.text: Perhaps young men's braggadocio is nothing more
Than nature's last defense against tyranny.
Else there'd be no war.
— John Petty, 1780

passage.text: Maybe not a poet, but not a thoughtless rooster, either. Later, Mercy placed his note between the pages of one of her old storybooks. That's when the idea for "Appeal" came to her. She was grateful; it had been a while since she'd had the urge to write poetry.
If she could improve "Appeal" to the point that it no longer disgusted her, she'd slip it to John when his company passed back through.
If they passed back through.

Against her will, Mercy pictured muskets and cannons. She shuddered, stuffing the poem back into her pocket. Most likely, she'd never see John again. Not in this bleak world, a world that didn't even deserve poetry. Regardless, she'd tarried too long. Quickly, she gathered the eggs, flung open the door—and blanched.

The sky appeared darker than when she'd entered the barn. Had her dark thoughts afflicted her vision? Mercy shook her head; what a notion! That's what came of stuffing her head with useless poetry. A storm was coming, that was all.
She carried the eggs to the kitchen, then joined her mother in serving the mush. They bade goodbye to the travelers, who were anxious to leave before the storm.
It grew ever darker as mother and daughter attended to their other chores. And yet, there was no thunder, no rain. At last, they could not deny that something was wrong.
Mercy and Mrs. Seely lit candles, then bowed their heads.
"Be steady," Mother whispered.
"Yes," Mercy whispered back.

By noon, it was as black as night. Villagers trickled into the tavern, wanting to know whether the whole of Connecticut was afflicted by darkness, but no travelers arrived to impart news. The villagers sat at the long table, their faces stricken in the candlelight. And then the night birds began to sing.
"Oh," breathed Mr. Cornwall. "Oh, mercy."
"Punishment, is what it is," Mr. Daly burst out.

"It's not, William," Mrs. Thomas said. She was a Patriot, while Mr. Daly was a Loyalist. Mercy had not seen them speak to each other in years. But now Mrs. Thomas gently placed a hand on Mr. Daly's arm, as tears streamed down his face. "Have faith," she whispered, tenderly. Gazing at them, Mercy thought of poetry again. Here was a living poem. Perhaps the world didn't deserve poetry—it was poetry.

Hundreds of miles away, wildfires were raging. Black smoke thickened, rose, and met a dense fog that had rolled in. The fog and smoke blotted out the sun. It was May 19, 1780, and the light went out of the world, however briefly. But in the village, in the oppressive darkness, an ember of hope grew.

The author can also communicate more subtle messages, such as the narrator's reliability, the passage's theme, or even the author's own attitudes.

As a result, you often need to make inferences to fully understand the story and the author's choices. When making inferences, use your background knowledge of the world to interpret the story's details. passage.text: Maybe not a poet, but not a thoughtless rooster, either. Later, Mercy placed his note between the pages of one of her old storybooks. That's when the idea for "Appeal" came to her. She was grateful; it had been a while since she'd had the urge to write poetry.
If she could improve "Appeal" to the point that it no longer disgusted her, she'd slip it to John when his company passed back through.
If they passed back through.

Against her will, Mercy pictured muskets and cannons. She shuddered, stuffing the poem back into her pocket. Most likely, she'd never see John again. Not in this bleak world, a world that didn't even deserve poetry. Regardless, she'd tarried too long. Quickly, she gathered the eggs, flung open the door—and blanched.

The sky appeared darker than when she'd entered the barn. Had her dark thoughts afflicted her vision? Mercy shook her head; what a notion! That's what came of stuffing her head with useless poetry. A storm was coming, that was all.
She carried the eggs to the kitchen, then joined her mother in serving the mush. They bade goodbye to the travelers, who were anxious to leave before the storm.
It grew ever darker as mother and daughter attended to their other chores. And yet, there was no thunder, no rain. At last, they could not deny that something was wrong.
Mercy and Mrs. Seely lit candles, then bowed their heads.
"Be steady," Mother whispered.
"Yes," Mercy whispered back.

By noon, it was as black as night. Villagers trickled into the tavern, wanting to know whether the whole of Connecticut was afflicted by darkness, but no travelers arrived to impart news. The villagers sat at the long table, their faces stricken in the candlelight. And then the night birds began to sing.
"Oh," breathed Mr. Cornwall. "Oh, mercy."
"Punishment, is what it is," Mr. Daly burst out.

"It's not, William," Mrs. Thomas said. She was a Patriot, while Mr. Daly was a Loyalist. Mercy had not seen them speak to each other in years. But now Mrs. Thomas gently placed a hand on Mr. Daly's arm, as tears streamed down his face. "Have faith," she whispered, tenderly. Gazing at them, Mercy thought of poetry again. Here was a living poem. Perhaps the world didn't deserve poetry—it was poetry.

Hundreds of miles away, wildfires were raging. Black smoke thickened, rose, and met a dense fog that had rolled in. The fog and smoke blotted out the sun. It was May 19, 1780, and the light went out of the world, however briefly. But in the village, in the oppressive darkness, an ember of hope grew.

header.text: <instructions>Read the story.</instructions>

passage.text: Knock, knock.

The child who lives in the trailer opposite my own is at my door. Her hair is so blonde, it's almost as white as mine, and it's jerked into a ponytail. Purple glasses. A darting, catlike quality to her movements. I remain, unconcerned, on the sofa with my book. She'll leave shortly, as she always does.
Knock, knock.

I suppose it's rude to ignore her like this, but in all likelihood, the child wants what I can't offer: a cliché. A comforting, grandmotherly type who bakes cookies and pats arms and…well, whatever else it is they do.
Knock, knock.
I realize I've read an entire paragraph without absorbing it. Irritated, I flick the page back.
Knock, knock, knock!

Now I slap my book down. The child wants a cliché? Fine. But she's not getting Grandma. She's getting Crone. I stride to the door, open it a crack, and scowl, expecting her to back off. Instead, she slinks through the sliver of open doorway. Did I mention she was catlike?
Catgirl stalks over to the sofa and settles herself there, placing her lavender backpack just so.
A voice calls, "Celia, I can't see you!"
"I don't need to be seen, Mother!" Catgirl's tone is indignant, like how cats would sound if they could speak.

"What do you mean, you don't need to be seen?" I snap. "You're nowhere near old enough for that luxury." I yank the door wide so that Catgirl's mother, standing in her own doorway, can see straight through to my couch. That's how close together these trailers are.

I expect the mother to say something like, "Catgirl, you come home this instant!" But she just appraises me, nods, and shuts her door. My mouth is literally hanging open at this point. What does the woman think I am, a free babysitter?

Folding my arms, I turn back to the scene in my living room. Catgirl, now clutching a notepad and pencil, gazes at me through her ludicrous eyewear. "I have a few questions," she snips, all Associated Press.
"Excuse me?"
"May I ask you a few questions, please."
"What is this, some sort of school project?"
She blinks. "Yes. Exactly. A history project."
Great. I'm history.
But five minutes of humoring her is certainly a fair price to pay for permanent privacy, so I lay down my terms. "After this? That's it. No more banging on my door. No impromptu visits. Agreed?"
Catgirl nods curtly and taps her pencil on the notepad, like she has nine other interviews to rush off to.
"Fine," I say. "Proceed."
She pounces. "What was your former identity?"
"Excuse me?"
"Let me rephrase. Who were you before the war?"
"What war?"
She squints at me like I'm under a microscope. "I think you know," she purrs. She pulls a book out of her backpack and presents it with a flourish. Spies of World War II: Hiding in Plain Sight.

Wow. Guess I was wrong about the Grandma cliché. I start laughing so hard that I have to put my hand on the kitchen table to steady myself. And I realize it's been a long time since I laughed. And then I remember that it's July. No school, no homework. No projects.
Poor Catgirl sits on my couch and watches me with a dismayed face, the ridiculous book sliding off her lap. Catgirl the spy. Thinking she's caught a fellow spy.

"I was a baby during World War II," I chortle. "How old do you imagine I am?" Catgirl looks confused at the thought that I was ever a baby. She opens her mouth, but I'm on a roll. "Before you investigate your next case," I start, putting "case" in air quotes, "you might want to bone up on common sense."

Catgirl's eyes fill—oh, criminy—and I drop my hands. She reaches for her backpack, but it topples, spilling notepads, pencils, and another book onto the floor. The Loneliness One Dare Not Sound: The Life of Emily Dickinson. Wait, Dickinson?

I watch her shoving everything back into the backpack, and now it's like I'm the one looking through the microscope. And I see her as she must actually be: a quirky, intelligent girl with a hopeless glut of imagination, stuck in a relentlessly lonely summer and creating a whole scenario about the odd old woman across the way. A woman who does, let's face it, have a past she wants to leave in the past. Celia wasn't all wrong.
I sigh, then walk over and sit on the other end of the sofa. "Okay, look," I say. "I'm sorry I laughed."
"Whatever," Celia mutters.
We lapse into silence, the emptiness of summer stretching in front of us.

passage.text: "Regular coffee is so last week. I only drink NCB now." Tom tosses his hair, then examines his imaginary manicure.
I laugh. His accent is a mash-up of Valley girl and faux-Parisian, which is not at all how Ms. Bely actually talks. But given how I've described her, I can't blame him for thinking so.
Mom pours herself coffee. "What's NCB?"
"Nitro cold brew," I say, trying out the same accent my brother used. "It's divine."
"It's iced coffee charged up with nitrogen," Tom explains in his regular voice. "I tried it once. It's actually not bad."

But I'm not ready to drop the impersonation, partly because I can't remember the last time my brother and I joked around at the breakfast table. Plus, I'm pretty good at the accent. "I always grab one after hot yoga," I say. "The juxtaposition of hot and cool is so thought-provoking."
Mom frowns. "Ada, is she really that insufferable? I thought she was nice."
"Anyone can be nice." I shrug. "What's insufferable is her shallowness. Her 'problems.' Her…meaninglessness."
"Nobody's meaningless."
"I don't know about that. Anyway, I just can't take people seriously who never do anything."
"What does she do when you babysit?" Tom asks.
This is new and amazing—Tom's interest in my life. Maybe he finally understands that I'm not a goofy, empty-headed kid anymore. I've changed a lot since he's been at college.

"Yoga, salon, whatever," I tell him, sticking my nose up the way I imagine Ms. Bely does. "Oh, she also hides out in her quote, unquote 'studio.'" I lean in conspiratorially. "The boys call it the 'mommy-time room.'"
Tom snorts, and I grin. Not goofily, I don't think.
"Well, she provides you with a paycheck," Mom says, pointing to the clock. Whoops, my shift is from nine to one. I grab my keys. "See you guys when I return from the Posh Side."
"Good luck," Tom says.

Raindrops splatter on my windshield as I park; we'll have to stay inside today. I picture the three of us in the playroom, crafting and playing board games. This is a sweet summer gig, I have to admit.
Aiden throws his arms around my waist as if it's been a year instead of just a day. "I had a toaster paste for breakfast!" I gently brush the crumbs off my mini-me's cheek.
"Toaster pastry," says Tony, his brother. "Paste is for sticking. Like what Mommy uses for—"
"I know what paste is!"
"No, 'cause you said—"
"Paste, what a great idea!" I exclaim. "That's what we'll do today. How about we make flags for July Fourth?"
They look at me, interest piqued. I've gotten good at this.
Ms. Bely dashes down the stairs. Peach running shoes, black yoga pants, black-and-gray scoop-neck shirt artfully layered over a peach tank. "How are you, Ada?"
"Good, how about you?"
"Great! I'll be back in a couple of hours." She kisses the boys, leaving peach lipstick on their cheeks. "Have fun, kids."
"We're doing paste, Mommy," Aiden says importantly. Tony and I exchange a smile.
"Sounds cool!" Ms. Bely winks at me before she leaves. False eyelashes for the gym, wow.
In the playroom, we pull construction paper, scissors, and glue out of the crafts box. "Tony, honey, this glue is nearly out. Is there more somewhere?"

"Why don't you ask me?" says Aiden. "I know, too. Anyway, you said paste." Aiden has scrambled up the climbing ladder that's bolted to the wall; he's eye-level with me now. "Paste, Ada, right? Not glue."
"Same thing," Tony and I say together, which makes us both laugh. "Let's try the closet," Tony says, pulling my hand.
The closet is stacked with bins. I pull down the one labeled papermaking. Tony and I spend about ten minutes carefully sorting through the bin. It's full of old magazines and junk mail, but no glue.
"We make homemade paper from this," Tony says.
"Really? Wait, where's Aiden?"
Tony shrugs, and I sigh. Sometimes Aiden hides under his bed. "Come on, Tony, let's go find him."
But he's nowhere in his bedroom.
"Aiden!" I call, walking through the house. Then louder. "Aiden!"
"Aiden! It's not funny!" Tony yells.

Suddenly, I hear a crash from below us. I race downstairs, into Ms. Bely's studio, which is open for some reason, and—oh. There's Aiden, dragging a huge plastic bucket of "acrylic gloss varnish" across the studio floor.
"Got the paste," he pants.
"You're not supposed to be in here without Mommy," Tony says, skidding into the room. "Right, Ada?"
But I don't answer, because I'm staring at the gigantic painting on the easel. No, it's not a painting, it's a collage. "Your mom's an artist?" I ask.
"Uh-huh," they say together.
I step closer. A woman holds a gigantic hourglass, and the sand is falling out and piling up around her feet. It's beyond me.
"Ada, let's make the flags," says Aiden.
"Give me one minute," I answer. I breathe deeply and stare into the hourglass woman's eyes, knowing that as soon as I stop, I'll have to face myself.

header.text: Review the twenty-ninth, thirtieth, and thirty-first paragraphs.

passage.text: "Regular coffee is so last week. I only drink NCB now." Tom tosses his hair, then examines his imaginary manicure.
I laugh. His accent is a mash-up of Valley girl and faux-Parisian, which is not at all how Ms. Bely actually talks. But given how I've described her, I can't blame him for thinking so.
Mom pours herself coffee. "What's NCB?"
"Nitro cold brew," I say, trying out the same accent my brother used. "It's divine."
"It's iced coffee charged up with nitrogen," Tom explains in his regular voice. "I tried it once. It's actually not bad."

But I'm not ready to drop the impersonation, partly because I can't remember the last time my brother and I joked around at the breakfast table. Plus, I'm pretty good at the accent. "I always grab one after hot yoga," I say. "The juxtaposition of hot and cool is so thought-provoking."
Mom frowns. "Ada, is she really that insufferable? I thought she was nice."
"Anyone can be nice." I shrug. "What's insufferable is her shallowness. Her 'problems.' Her…meaninglessness."
"Nobody's meaningless."
"I don't know about that. Anyway, I just can't take people seriously who never do anything."
"What does she do when you babysit?" Tom asks.
This is new and amazing—Tom's interest in my life. Maybe he finally understands that I'm not a goofy, empty-headed kid anymore. I've changed a lot since he's been at college.

"Yoga, salon, whatever," I tell him, sticking my nose up the way I imagine Ms. Bely does. "Oh, she also hides out in her quote, unquote 'studio.'" I lean in conspiratorially. "The boys call it the 'mommy-time room.'"
Tom snorts, and I grin. Not goofily, I don't think.
"Well, she provides you with a paycheck," Mom says, pointing to the clock. Whoops, my shift is from nine to one. I grab my keys. "See you guys when I return from the Posh Side."
"Good luck," Tom says.

Raindrops splatter on my windshield as I park; we'll have to stay inside today. I picture the three of us in the playroom, crafting and playing board games. This is a sweet summer gig, I have to admit.
Aiden throws his arms around my waist as if it's been a year instead of just a day. "I had a toaster paste for breakfast!" I gently brush the crumbs off my mini-me's cheek.
"Toaster pastry," says Tony, his brother. "Paste is for sticking. Like what Mommy uses for—"
"I know what paste is!"
"No, 'cause you said—"
"Paste, what a great idea!" I exclaim. "That's what we'll do today. How about we make flags for July Fourth?"
They look at me, interest piqued. I've gotten good at this.
Ms. Bely dashes down the stairs. Peach running shoes, black yoga pants, black-and-gray scoop-neck shirt artfully layered over a peach tank. "How are you, Ada?"
"Good, how about you?"
"Great! I'll be back in a couple of hours." She kisses the boys, leaving peach lipstick on their cheeks. "Have fun, kids."
"We're doing paste, Mommy," Aiden says importantly. Tony and I exchange a smile.
"Sounds cool!" Ms. Bely winks at me before she leaves. False eyelashes for the gym, wow.
In the playroom, we pull construction paper, scissors, and glue out of the crafts box. "Tony, honey, this glue is nearly out. Is there more somewhere?"

"Why don't you ask me?" says Aiden. "I know, too. Anyway, you said paste." Aiden has scrambled up the climbing ladder that's bolted to the wall; he's eye-level with me now. "Paste, Ada, right? Not glue."
"Same thing," Tony and I say together, which makes us both laugh. "Let's try the closet," Tony says, pulling my hand.
The closet is stacked with bins. I pull down the one labeled papermaking. Tony and I spend about ten minutes carefully sorting through the bin. It's full of old magazines and junk mail, but no glue.
"We make homemade paper from this," Tony says.
"Really? Wait, where's Aiden?"
Tony shrugs, and I sigh. Sometimes Aiden hides under his bed. "Come on, Tony, let's go find him."
But he's nowhere in his bedroom.
"Aiden!" I call, walking through the house. Then louder. "Aiden!"
"Aiden! It's not funny!" Tony yells.

Suddenly, I hear a crash from below us. I race downstairs, into Ms. Bely's studio, which is open for some reason, and—oh. There's Aiden, dragging a huge plastic bucket of "acrylic gloss varnish" across the studio floor.
"Got the paste," he pants.
"You're not supposed to be in here without Mommy," Tony says, skidding into the room. "Right, Ada?"
But I don't answer, because I'm staring at the gigantic painting on the easel. No, it's not a painting, it's a collage. "Your mom's an artist?" I ask.
"Uh-huh," they say together.
I step closer. A woman holds a gigantic hourglass, and the sand is falling out and piling up around her feet. It's beyond me.
"Ada, let's make the flags," says Aiden.
"Give me one minute," I answer. I breathe deeply and stare into the hourglass woman's eyes, knowing that as soon as I stop, I'll have to face myself.

passage.text: As he parks, my father says, "Leah. About Madison. She's not exactly…herself."
I busy myself with the door handle. "Yeah. I mean, hard place to be. The hospital."
"And also, when she comes home. The adjusting."
"Right."
My father and I both tend to speak in staccato when we're nervous.
We walk toward the medical center, and I consider his phrasing: "Not exactly herself." I wonder if she even cares. Maybe she's happy to cast off her old self. To molt.

Like that time at the Turvy Street Festival. We'd gone together, just the two of us. Booths full of pottery and batik and beaded jewelry. The smell of sugar and grease. We had just split a funnel cake, and Madison had gone to throw away the plate. She came running back. "Leah, there's a free haircut booth!"

"Nothing's free," I said. She laughed, grabbed my hand, and pointed to a plastic banner: Free Cuts from À L'envers Salon! The bouncing hairdresser spied us immediately and cried, "Ladies! Let Pierre transform you!"

"Let's go," I muttered, but Madison was already jumping into the chair and requesting "something radical." Pierre's scissors flashed; his razor whirred. The two of them chatted like soul mates. Fifteen minutes later, he triumphantly spun her chair around to face the mirror. She stared at her reflection. "I'm gone," she breathed. I shuddered, but Not-Madison didn't notice. She flung her arms around Pierre, then plopped a ten-dollar tip into his hand. The last of her money.
Now I shudder again, and my father touches my shoulder. "I mean, why would she have thought it was a good idea to—" I cut myself off.
My father says, "This might not be the best time—"
"I know. Forget it."
And suddenly, we're in the lobby, the elevators yawning open.
I stop walking. "We should get a coffee," I say. "For Mom. Shouldn't we?"
Dad nods. "All right." We turn from the elevators.

The cafeteria: salads in cellophane, fries wilting under heat lamps, aluminum vats of coffee. Dad and I deliberate over caffeine, sweetener, dairy. There are two lines for the cashier, one on either side of her. She takes turns so that the lines will stay even, but they aren't. I make sure we join the longer one, my father holding one cup of regular and one cup of decaf, me clutching packets of sugar, sweetener, creamer. So many choices.

"Just choose!" I can hear Madison saying. And I remember plastic yellow ducks floating in a tub of greasy water, state fair music, my parents laughing. Ten years ago? Twelve? We were playing one of those rigged carnival games—the one where you get to catch a duck with a fishing pole, then exchange it for a prize.

Madison caught her duck within three seconds. The barker unhooked it, flicked his eyes over the label on the bottom, and shouted, "Goldilocks here just won herself a spider ring!" Madison was so proud of that ring, twisting it around her index finger and grinning. But I didn't want a dud prize. I wanted the plushy purple dog that no one ever won. I stared at the revolving ducks. One of them was right, but which? My hands were sweating as I gripped the pole. Did I ever even choose? I don't remember. I only remember Madison jumping up and down, yelling, "Choose! Choose! Leah, just choose!"

The elevator dings, and my father and I step out, carefully balancing our coffee suite. We walk down the hall, past the nurses' station, past closed door after closed door, until finally my father stops at Madison's.
"Dad," I say.
He turns.
"I need the restroom. Here." I dump the creamers and sweeteners into his jacket pocket. I don't even open the door for him.

The restroom: banging doors, mirrors under unforgiving lights. I stare at the circles under my eyes. I could text him: Not feeling well. Will wait for you in lobby, no, in front of hospital, no, in parking garage, no, in the closet at home.

I found Madison there once, in the coat closet by the living room. About five years ago. It was the day she brought Impulse home—mangy, scrawny, abandoned. I opened the closet to hang my jacket, and there she was, arms around him as he trembled.
I screamed, and Impulse barked. Madison shushed me.
"Cutie needs darkness and quiet," she murmured. "Come in." But I didn't. I just closed the door, remembering that I had seen him, too, just the day before, skulking in the bushes.
Impulse—or Cutie, as only Madison calls him—has been hiding under her bed for the past two days. I still don't know how to help him.

I wash my hands, slowly dry them on rough paper towels. Finally, I leave the restroom, stand in the hall. The elevators are ahead, Madison's room off to my right. And I close my eyes against the burden of choice.

"Nothing's free," I said. She laughed, grabbed my hand, and pointed to a plastic banner: Free Cuts from À L'envers Salon! The bouncing hairdresser spied us immediately and cried, "Ladies! Let Pierre transform you!"

"Let's go," I muttered, but Madison was already jumping into the chair and requesting "something radical." Pierre's scissors flashed; his razor whirred. The two of them chatted like soul mates. Fifteen minutes later, he triumphantly spun her chair around to face the mirror. She stared at her reflection. "I'm gone," she breathed. I shuddered, but Not-Madison didn't notice. She flung her arms around Pierre, then plopped a ten-dollar tip into his hand. The last of her money.
Now I shudder again, and my father touches my shoulder. "I mean, why would she have thought it was a good idea to—" I cut myself off.
My father says, "This might not be the best time—"
"I know. Forget it."
And suddenly, we're in the lobby, the elevators yawning open.
I stop walking. "We should get a coffee," I say. "For Mom. Shouldn't we?"
Dad nods. "All right." We turn from the elevators.

There are two lines for the cashier, one on either side of her. She takes turns so that the lines will stay even, but they aren't. I make sure we join the longer one, my father holding one cup of regular and one cup of decaf, me clutching packets of sugar, sweetener, creamer. So many choices.

"Just choose!" I can hear Madison saying. And I remember plastic yellow ducks floating in a tub of greasy water, state fair music, my parents laughing. Ten years ago? Twelve? We were playing one of those rigged carnival games—the one where you get to catch a duck with a fishing pole, then exchange it for a prize.

Madison caught her duck within three seconds. The barker unhooked it, flicked his eyes over the label on the bottom, and shouted, "Goldilocks here just won herself a spider ring!" Madison was so proud of that ring, twisting it around her index finger and grinning. But I didn't want a dud prize. I wanted the plushy purple dog that no one ever won. I stared at the revolving ducks. One of them was right, but which? My hands were sweating as I gripped the pole. Did I ever even choose? I don't remember. I only remember Madison jumping up and down, yelling, "Choose! Choose! Leah, just choose!"

The elevator dings, and my father and I step out, carefully balancing our coffee suite. We walk down the hall, past the nurses' station, past closed door after closed door, until finally my father stops at Madison's.
"Dad," I say.
He turns.
"I need the restroom. Here." I dump the creamers and sweeteners into his jacket pocket. I don't even open the door for him.

The restroom: banging doors, mirrors under unforgiving lights. I stare at the circles under my eyes. I could text him: Not feeling well. Will wait for you in lobby, no, in front of hospital, no, in parking garage, no, in the closet at home.

I found Madison there once, in the coat closet by the living room. About five years ago. It was the day she brought Impulse home—mangy, scrawny, abandoned. I opened the closet to hang my jacket, and there she was, arms around him as he trembled.
I screamed, and Impulse barked. Madison shushed me.
"Cutie needs darkness and quiet," she murmured. "Come in." But I didn't. I just closed the door, remembering that I had seen him, too, just the day before, skulking in the bushes.
Impulse—or Cutie, as only Madison calls him—has been hiding under her bed for the past two days. I still don't know how to help him.

I wash my hands, slowly dry them on rough paper towels. Finally, I leave the restroom, stand in the hall. The elevators are ahead, Madison's room off to my right. And I close my eyes against the burden of choice.

passage.text: A throng of passengers got off at the Division Street stop, so Masha and Molly were finally able to sit.
"Ah, that's better," Molly said. "Now we can talk. Masha, come to the presentation tonight. Please. It's not a social thing. It's educational!"
The streetcar swayed, and Masha grabbed Molly's arm to steady herself. "I already told you," she said. "I can't."
"Can't!" Molly waved her hands as if batting away a fly. "Of course you can. No work tomorrow, remember? Relax for once! Do something fun."
"I am. Mama and I are baking rugelach." Seeing Molly's confused expression, Masha explained, "It's a dessert."
Molly waved her hand again. "Rosie can help her."
"Rosie!" Masha laughed.
"Why not? I bet you made roo-gla at her age."
"Rosie isn't interested. She's an American. And it's rugelach, not 'roo-gla.' You make it sound like a dance."

"See, now that would be fun." Molly deepened her voice. "Ladies and gentlemen! Presenting the roo-gla, the hottest dance of 1920!" She giggled. "Anyway, what are you even saying? You're American, too. You live here, don't you?"

"Yes, but Rosie is…of here." Masha's younger sister wore sailor-style blouses, owned a dozen ribbons for her bobbed hair, and knew all the latest songs. The heady aroma of yeast and nuts could never transport her back to their homeland, which Rosie barely remembered. As far as Rosie was concerned, America was their homeland. Whoops, Molly was talking.
"—just as American as she is. As American as apple pie! Come with me, Masha, and I'll bake an apple pie for your mama. You don't need roo-gla." Molly paused. "Ru-ge-lach."
Masha fell back against the seat, laughing. But then she sat up. "Wait a minute, Molly. Why are you so keen on this lecture?"

"I'm very interested in ancient art," Molly said. She tossed her copper curls and gazed at Masha with wide-eyed innocence. Masha stared back, eyes narrowed. Finally, Molly threw up her hands. "I overheard Stephen talking, and—"
"Aha! So Stephen will be there, will he?" Masha tossed her own hair in an imitation of Molly. "I'm very interested in ancient art," she squeaked.
They collapsed into laughter. "Okay, okay." Molly wiped her eyes. "Now will you come? Who knows, maybe you'll meet a young man!" She elbowed Masha. "Someone you can bake roo-gla for."
"Don't be silly. The last thing I want is to spend my life cooking for some old-world husband."
"See! You're more American than you think!"

It was true. If Masha ever returned to the old country, she wouldn't fit in. Nor, she realized suddenly, would she want to. And yet, she didn't want to wear a bob either. Or eat apple pie. She wanted rugelach. And borscht. And to sing the old folk songs to her children. If, that is, she remembered them by the time she had children. She rubbed her temples.
"What's wrong?" Molly asked.
"Do you remember Ireland?"
"Not much, no. Do you remember Poland?"
"Just fragments," Masha said. "I don't want to let go of them."
"Ah." There was understanding in Molly's eyes. "They're part of you, those fragments."

"Yes. Yes, exactly." Masha squeezed Molly's hand as the streetcar swayed again. Despite all their differences, Molly was the best friend Masha had ever had. Molly understood her. "Okay, Molly. I'll come with you," Masha said.
"Oh, Masha, thank you! And you know what, I bet you'll like it more than I do!"
Masha shook her head, already missing the smell of the rugelach dough. She wondered whether her mother would mind.
But Mama was thrilled. "Wonderful, Masha, you need to go out more!"
Rosie came running. "Masha, try my blue dress. And let me put some rouge on your cheeks. No, don't rub it off. Honestly!"
When Molly came by, she pretended to fall over. "Look who's modern now! Seriously, Masha, you're beautiful."
As they walked arm in arm up Unity Street, Masha did feel relaxed. Maybe it was a good thing, getting out sometimes.

When they stepped into the Alliance lobby, Masha gazed around in amazement. "Wait until you see the lecture room," Molly said, pulling her along. It was a classroom, really, but airy and beautifully lit. Masha and Molly took seats near the front, where Stephen was sitting. Molly waved to him, her eyes rounded in a perfect simulation of surprise.

"Welcome to Unity Street Alliance!" The lecturer smiled. "Tonight we'll discuss an art form called mosaic, which has flourished since ancient times." She paused. "I like to think of it as the art of fragments. Here is one of my own attempts, amateur though it may be." She held up a board on which varied bits of ceramic were arranged to form a cohesive design. Masha stared, hand on her heart.
After a few moments, the woman returned the board to her lectern. "Let's begin with the Roman Empire…"
Masha glanced at Molly, who was sitting up straight, cheeks flushed. Masha suspected that her own expression was similarly exuberant.

"—just as American as she is. As American as apple pie! Come with me, Masha, and I'll bake an apple pie for your mama. You don't need roo-gla." Molly paused. "Ru-ge-lach."
Masha fell back against the seat, laughing. But then she sat up. "Wait a minute, Molly. Why are you so keen on this lecture?"

"I'm very interested in ancient art," Molly said. She tossed her copper curls and gazed at Masha with wide-eyed innocence. Masha stared back, eyes narrowed. Finally, Molly threw up her hands. "I overheard Stephen talking, and—"
"Aha! So Stephen will be there, will he?" Masha tossed her own hair in an imitation of Molly. "I'm very interested in ancient art," she squeaked.
They collapsed into laughter. "Okay, okay." Molly wiped her eyes. "Now will you come? Who knows, maybe you'll meet a young man!" She elbowed Masha. "Someone you can bake roo-gla for."
"Don't be silly. The last thing I want is to spend my life cooking for some old-world husband."
"See! You're more American than you think!"

It was true. If Masha ever returned to the old country, she wouldn't fit in. Nor, she realized suddenly, would she want to. And yet, she didn't want to wear a bob either. Or eat apple pie. She wanted rugelach. And borscht. And to sing the old folk songs to her children. If, that is, she remembered them by the time she had children. She rubbed her temples.
"What's wrong?" Molly asked.
"Do you remember Ireland?"
"Not much, no. Do you remember Poland?"
"Just fragments," Masha said. "I don't want to let go of them."
"Ah." There was understanding in Molly's eyes. "They're part of you, those fragments."

"Yes. Yes, exactly." Masha squeezed Molly's hand as the streetcar swayed again. Despite all their differences, Molly was the best friend Masha had ever had. Molly understood her. "Okay, Molly. I'll come with you," Masha said.
"Oh, Masha, thank you! And you know what, I bet you'll like it more than I do!"
Masha shook her head, already missing the smell of the rugelach dough. She wondered whether her mother would mind.
But Mama was thrilled. "Wonderful, Masha, you need to go out more!"
Rosie came running. "Masha, try my blue dress. And let me put some rouge on your cheeks. No, don't rub it off. Honestly!"
When Molly came by, she pretended to fall over. "Look who's modern now! Seriously, Masha, you're beautiful."
As they walked arm in arm up Unity Street, Masha did feel relaxed. Maybe it was a good thing, getting out sometimes.

When they stepped into the Alliance lobby, Masha gazed around in amazement. "Wait until you see the lecture room," Molly said, pulling her along. It was a classroom, really, but airy and beautifully lit. Masha and Molly took seats near the front, where Stephen was sitting. Molly waved to him, her eyes rounded in a perfect simulation of surprise.

"Welcome to Unity Street Alliance!" The lecturer smiled. "Tonight we'll discuss an art form called mosaic, which has flourished since ancient times." She paused. "I like to think of it as the art of fragments. Here is one of my own attempts, amateur though it may be." She held up a board on which varied bits of ceramic were arranged to form a cohesive design. Masha stared, hand on her heart.
After a few moments, the woman returned the board to her lectern. "Let's begin with the Roman Empire…"
Masha glanced at Molly, who was sitting up straight, cheeks flushed. Masha suspected that her own expression was similarly exuberant.

She realizes that her "fragmented" identity is a thing to be appreciated.

contents.text: The author doesn't always tell you everything in a story. For example, he or she often merely suggests events, settings, and character traits. The author can also communicate more subtle messages, such as the narrator's reliability, the passage's theme, or even the author's own attitudes.

As a result, you often need to make inferences to fully understand the story and the author's choices. When making inferences, use your background knowledge of the world to interpret the story's details. Also, pay attention to the story's imagery, structure, and other stylistic elements, and consider what purpose they serve. Remember to base your inferences on evidence from the text.

header.text: <instructions>The following passage describes the bathing habits of people in 19th-century England. Select the best evidence to support the statement "bathwater was a shared resource in 19th-century homes." There may be more than one correct choice.</instructions>

text.text: <atomic>In the early part of the nineteenth century, you would have been well advised to stand upwind of anyone with whom you were having a conversation.</atomic>
<atomic>Only the hands, neck and arms were frequently washed.</atomic>
<atomic>The poor must have bathed infrequently at best.</atomic>

<atomic>The middle class, although they apparently washed their hands and feet daily, usually made do in the 1860s with one big bath on Sunday night, in which the whole household took part, perhaps because it was such a nuisance to boil all that water.</atomic>
<atomic>And at Mrs. Browning's Academy in Blackheath for young ladies a weekly bath was charged as an extra.</atomic>
<atomic>Partly this was due to a lack of readily available water.</atomic>
<atomic>In the countryside, water came from streams, rivers, wells, or…pumps.</atomic>

By drawing upon such evidence, you make your writing more accurate. In addition, by quoting or citing such evidence when appropriate, you avoid plagiarism and make your writing more convincing.

header.text: <instructions>Select the best evidence to support the statement "The task of returning art stolen during World War II continued long after the end of the war." There may be more than one correct choice.</instructions>

text.text: During Germany's conquest of Europe, a Nazi party group known as the Einsatzstab Reichsleiter Rosenberg (or ERR) stole millions of paintings, manuscripts, sculptures, furniture, and other cultural materials.
These artifacts were slated either for destruction or to be displayed in a future Führermuseum.
<atomic>In the final months of World War II and continuing for years afterward, the Monuments Men worked to protect these treasures and return them to their rightful owners.</atomic>
<atomic>In the war's aftermath, the Monuments Men were aided by the discovery of thirty-nine photo albums created by the ERR documenting their theft.</atomic>
<atomic>These albums also served as evidence during the Nuremburg Trials as proof of the massive Nazi art looting operations.</atomic>
<atomic>These thirty-nine albums are now part of the National Archives.</atomic>

contents.text: <citation>Adapted from Christopher Zarr, "Records of the Monuments Men at the National Archives"</citation>

header.text: <instructions>Select the best evidence to support the statement "Eleanor Roosevelt's relationship with the media was unlike that of any first lady before her." There may be more than one correct choice.</instructions>

text.text: <atomic>When Mrs. Roosevelt came to the White House in 1933,</atomic>
<atomic>she understood social conditions better than any of her predecessors and she transformed the role of first lady accordingly.</atomic>
<atomic>She never shirked official entertaining; she greeted thousands with charming friendliness.</atomic>

<atomic>She also broke precedent to hold press conferences, travel to all parts of the country, give lectures and radio broadcasts, and express her opinions candidly in a daily syndicated newspaper column, "My Day."</atomic>

<atomic>This made her a tempting target for political enemies but her integrity, her graciousness, and her sincerity of purpose endeared her personally to many—from heads of state to servicemen she visited abroad during World War II.</atomic>

header.text: <instructions>Select the best evidence to support the statement "The United Farm Workers of America served more than just farm workers." There may be more than one correct choice.</instructions>

text.text: <atomic>Under the leadership of César E. Chávez and others such as Dolores Huerta and Larry Itliong, along with support from millions of Americans,</atomic>
<atomic>the farm worker movement joined forces with other reform movements to achieve unprecedented successes that greatly improved working and living conditions and wages for farm workers.</atomic>

<atomic>During the 1970s the United Farm Workers of America (UFW) grew and expanded from its early roots as a union for farm workers to also become a national voice for the poor and disenfranchised.</atomic>

<atomic>The enduring legacies of César E. Chávez and the farm worker movement include passage of California's Agricultural Labor Relations Act of 1975, the first law in the U.S. that recognized farm workers' collective bargaining rights.</atomic>

<atomic>Saturn's moon Titan is famous for its methane, which can exist not only as a liquid and gas at Titan's surface temperatures and pressures, but also as solid ice.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Most of Monet's paintings from the 1870s depict the landscape in and around the small towns along the Seine.</atomic>
<atomic>Working outdoors, he employed seemingly spontaneous brushstrokes to capture the ever-changing effects of light and atmosphere.</atomic>
<atomic>In the 1880s Monet expanded his motifs, turning his attention both to the Mediterranean and to the rugged vistas along the Normandy coast.</atomic>
<atomic>In the 1890s he undertook a number of paintings produced in series,</atomic>
<atomic>including pictures of poplars, grainstacks, and Rouen Cathedral;</atomic>
<atomic>each work captured a specific atmospheric effect and time of day.</atomic>
<atomic>With his reputation as France's leading landscape painter established and his financial situation secure,</atomic>
<atomic>the artist turned his attention to the lavish gardens he had constructed at Giverny, eventually creating more than 250 works focused on water lilies.</atomic>

contents.text: Most of Monet's paintings from the 1870s depict the landscape in and around the small towns along the Seine. Working outdoors, he employed seemingly spontaneous brushstrokes to capture the ever-changing effects of light and atmosphere. In the 1880s Monet expanded his motifs, turning his attention both to the Mediterranean and to the rugged vistas along the Normandy coast. In the 1890s he undertook a number of paintings produced in series, including pictures of poplars, grainstacks, and Rouen Cathedral; each work captured a specific atmospheric effect and time of day. With his reputation as France's leading landscape painter established and his financial situation secure, the artist turned his attention to the lavish gardens he had constructed at Giverny, eventually creating more than 250 works focused on water lilies.
According to the text, Monet's brushstrokes, which appear "seemingly spontaneous," were actually an attempt to capture the "ever-changing," or transitory, characteristics of light and atmosphere.

contents.text: Caroline Bingley's attention was quite as much engaged in watching Mr. Darcy's progress through his book, as in reading her own; and she was perpetually either making some inquiry, or looking at his page. She could not win him, however, to any conversation; he merely answered her question, and read on. At length, quite exhausted by the attempt to be amused with her own book, which she had only chosen because it was the second volume of his, she gave a great yawn and said, "How pleasant it is to spend an evening in this way! I declare after all there is no enjoyment like reading! How much sooner one tires of any thing than of a book! When I have a house of my own, I shall be miserable if I have not an excellent library."
According to the passage, despite Caroline's interest in Mr. Darcy, Darcy is unwilling to engage with Caroline in any more than a polite, perfunctory way.

contents.text: Jem condescended to take me to school the first day, a job usually done by one's parents, but Atticus had said Jem would be delighted to show me where my room was. I think some money changed hands in this transaction, for as we trotted around the corner past the Radley Place I heard an unfamiliar jingle in Jem's pockets. When we slowed to a walk at the edge of the schoolyard, Jem was careful to explain that during school hours I was not to bother him, I was not to approach him with requests to enact a chapter of Tarzan and the Ant Men, to embarrass him with references to his private life, or tag along behind him at recess and noon.

Though Atticus claims that Jem is happy to take Scout to school, Scout suspects that "some money changed hands in this transaction." She hears coins jingling in Jem's pockets and assumes Atticus paid Jem to walk with her to school.

header.text: <instructions>Select the best evidence to support the statement "The narrator's father is a calm and secure man." There may be more than one correct choice.</instructions>

text.text: <atomic>The tiny share we have of time appalls me,</atomic>
<atomic>though my father seems to regard it with tranquillity.</atomic>
<atomic>Even my father, who sometimes seems to me to have been at home in the world as long as it has lasted,</atomic>
<atomic>has really lived on this earth only a little longer than I have,</atomic>
<atomic>in terms of all the time there has been to live in.</atomic>
<atomic>He has not known a time, any more than I, when automobiles and electric lights did not at least exist.</atomic>
<atomic>He was not alive when this century started.</atomic>
<atomic>I will be barely alive—old, old—when it ends. I do not like to think of it.</atomic>

header.text: <instructions>In the following passage, author James M. Cain gives his view of Los Angeles during the 1930s. Select the best evidence to support the statement "The author believes that diversity will be a boon to Los Angeles culture." There may be more than one correct choice.</instructions>

text.text: <atomic>Where this place is headed is to be the leader</atomic>
<atomic>in commerce, art, citrus production, music, rabbit breeding, oil production, furniture manufacture, walnut growing,</atomic>
<atomic>literature, olive bottling, short- and long-distance hauling, clay modelling, aesthetic criticism, fish export,</atomic>
<atomic>canary-bird culture, playwrighting, shipping, cinematic creativeness, and drawing-room manners.</atomic>
<atomic>In short, it is going to be a paradise on earth.</atomic>
<atomic>And, with such vaulting ambitions, it might pull off something: you can't tell.</atomic>
<atomic>It is keenly aware of Asia, and also of Mexico; streams are meeting here that ought to churn up some exciting whirlpools.</atomic>
<atomic>I, personally, even if the first act hasn't been so hot, am not going to walk out on the show.</atomic>

header.text: <instructions>Select the best evidence to support the statement "Financial incentives from the federal government are partly responsible for the growth in wind energy in the United States." There may be more than one correct choice.</instructions>

text.text: <atomic>From 2008 to 2014, the United States led all other countries in the amount of electricity generated by wind.</atomic>

<atomic>about three times more than the wind power generated in the United States in 2008.</atomic>
<atomic>A major contributor to increasing U.S. wind power in recent years has been the federal production tax credit.</atomic>
<atomic>The amount of U.S. electricity generated from wind has also increased because of state governments' renewable portfolio standards</atomic>
<atomic>that require a percentage of their states' electricity supply to come from wind power and other renewable energy sources.</atomic>

header.text: <instructions>Select the best evidence to support the statement "There has been a large increase in the number of earthquakes since the 1970s." There may be more than one correct choice.</instructions>

text.text: <atomic>Within the central and eastern United States, the number of earthquakes has changed dramatically over the past few years.</atomic>
<atomic>Between the years 1973–2008, there was an average of twenty-one earthquakes of magnitude three and larger in the central and eastern United States.</atomic>
<atomic>This rate jumped to an average of ninety-nine magnitude three or larger earthquakes per year in 2009–2013, and the rate continues to rise.</atomic>
<atomic>In 2014, alone, there were 659 magnitude three and larger earthquakes.</atomic>
<atomic>Most of these earthquakes are in the magnitude 3–4 range, large enough to have been felt by many people, yet small enough to rarely cause damage.</atomic>
<atomic>The change in the number of earthquakes prompts two important questions:</atomic>
<atomic>first, are the earthquakes natural or manmade?</atomic>
<atomic>Second, what should be done in the future as we address the causes and consequences of these events to reduce associated risks?</atomic>

header.text: <instructions>Select the best evidence to support the statement "John Harvard did not anticipate that a university would be named after him." There may be more than one correct choice.</instructions>

text.text: John Harvard did not found Harvard University, as is commonly believed.
<atomic>The Puritans founded it collectively in 1636 with a public grant of four hundred pounds for the purpose of training young ministers of the gospel.</atomic>
<atomic>The university, however, honors the name of John Harvard, a butcher's son and a graduate of Cambridge University.</atomic>
<atomic>He died in 1638 of tuberculosis, bequeathing a modest sum of money along with four hundred books—his entire library—to the institution.</atomic>
<atomic>Little did young Harvard dream of the fame to be attached to his name for this modest act of charity.</atomic>
<atomic>And even less could he have dreamed that his little library of four hundred books would one day increase to more than eight million.</atomic>

contents.text: John Harvard did not found Harvard University, as is commonly believed. The university, however, honors the name of John Harvard, a butcher's son and a graduate of Cambridge University. He died in 1638 of tuberculosis, bequeathing a modest sum of money along with four hundred books—his entire library—to the institution.
